Though it may seem, to one standing at the threshold of the old orchard, that nothing lies beyond but shadows and the interlacing of tired apple limbs, there is, in fact, a kind of glory woven through those branches, a quiet that waits not for permission to please but for the gentle patience of someone willing to notice the way the light drips like honey down the furrowed bark, pooling in golden puddles where moss grows thick and the scent of last season’s leaves mingles with the promise of bloom. There are things, I suppose, that can be counted and measured: the number of apples that fell last autumn and rotted sweetly into the soil, the steps from the gate to the gnarled tree at the center, the length of the laughter that once echoed beneath these trees from throats far too young to understand the fleeting nature of their joy, but there are other things, pleasures that slip between the moments and are gone, unnumbered and unnamed, though they leave an aftertaste on the tongue and a shiver in the blood that lingers long after the orchard is lost beneath twilight’s hush.

It may be that to please is to give, and that the giving is not always recognized for the glory it brings. I have watched the wind tumble petals across the grass, watched a blackbird clatter through the branches with a cry that is neither warning nor invitation but simply a declaration of presence: I am here, and that is enough. It is not always what we want—these moments drift past, unnoticed, while we wait for something larger, some thunderous revelation of meaning, but in their passing, they remind us that nothing, perhaps, is more glorious than the small, unheralded pleasures that stitch our days together. The glint of sun on an apple just beyond reach; the slow, sensual stretch of the roots beneath your feet, silent and relentless; the way your fingers, if you let them linger against the rough bark, begin to remember all the things you have touched and lost and longed for, as if the tree itself might please you with a secret whispered through time.

In the orchard’s heart, where the oldest tree’s limbs reach not up but outward, embracing everything it can, there stands a stone, half-buried in earth and lichen, a marker of something that once mattered to someone, though their name and purpose have vanished as surely as spring fades into summer’s heat. I have sat beside that stone many afternoons, tracing its pitted surface, feeling the slow pulse of history and loss beneath my palm, and wondered if the pleasure we seek is not so much in the things themselves as in the act of noticing them, the glory of attention paid to what is otherwise overlooked. There is a kind of reverence in this, a quiet glory that asks nothing but to be witnessed, to live in the silent exchange between moment and memory.

May you, too, find your way into such places, where nothing is demanded but everything is offered, where glory does not announce itself but waits, patient as moss or the slow twist of a root reclaiming earth. The days are full of things we may never understand, and maybe that is as it must be. To please, to be pleased, is not always to possess or to name, but to surrender for a breath, a heartbeat, a lingering taste on the tongue that says yes, this is enough. The orchard grows as it always has, indifferent to what we think we want or need, offering its shadows and its light, its bruised fruit and its tangled roots, and in so doing, reminding us that perhaps the greatest pleasure, the truest glory, lies in the acceptance of things as they are—imperfect, fleeting, but utterly real.

One day, when the orchard is grown wild and the stone is swallowed entirely by earth, someone may wander here and feel, without knowing why, that they are being watched by something kind and old and pleased to share this quiet ruin with them. They may stand at the threshold, hesitate, and then step forward, surrendered to the hush and the gold and the strange, sweet certainty that though nothing lasts, everything matters in the moment it is seen, and that is glory enough for any life.

In the old house at the corner of Maple and 3rd, where the paint peeled like shedding snakeskin and the porch sagged from years of sighing under winter snow, lived Mr. Statler, or Old Statler as the children called him with the kind of wary reverence that old men tend to inspire in young hearts unacquainted with the wear of time. He had not always been old, though to those who saw him now, with his knobby hands and his beard gone bristly white, it seemed impossible that he had ever been any other way. He moved slowly, it is true, as if every step cost him a decision, but his eyes, at certain moments, could flash with the green quickness of a spring-lit forest, and then one glimpsed the man he had been, living still beneath the folds of age.

Those who delivered the mail spoke quietly of the inside of the house, saying it smelled of pipe tobacco and oiled leather, and that the walls bore maps—dozens of them—of cities and coastlines, rivers and mountain chains, as if Old Statler was keeping track of the world’s changing face for some purpose known only to himself. The children, when their balls or kites escaped into his yard, would sometimes dart up onto the porch and peer through the wavy glass, and on good days, Old Statler would open the door and invite them in without speaking, his gesture crooked but warm, to retrieve whatever they had lost. Sometimes he would let them linger, and point out a country with a gnarled finger, muttering, “Here be tigers, methinks,” or “In the valleys here, the air smells like honey and thunder.” The children would giggle, unsure if he was teasing or telling the truth, and scamper away when they felt the weight of his gaze.

It was said by some—those who remembered him as the young man who had once left town with a knapsack and a grin as wide as the river—that Old Statler had lived a life that ran richer and deeper than most, and that he kept those maps as a kind of journal, each line and symbol a memory pressed flat and silent for safekeeping. There were rumors that he had fought in wars, that he had sailed on ships with names as forgettable as dreams, that he had loved and lost and loved again, all while the rest of the town went about its cycles of planting and reaping, loving and dying, as ordinary as the seasons themselves.

His daughter sometimes visited, driving up from the city in a car so new and polished it looked absurd parked beside the faded clapboard. She would bring groceries, sometimes a pie or a tin of coffee, and would sit with Old Statler on the porch, trying in her careful and adult way to persuade him to move in with her, “just for a little while, Dad, until it’s easier.” But he would only smile, his face softening like wet clay, and say, “There are still places on the map I’ve yet to visit, even if only with my mind.” She would sigh, not really understanding—how could she?—yet love and resignation mingled in her eyes as she kissed his forehead and returned to her world of schedules and elevators.

The people in town marked the passing of Old Statler’s days as one marks the seasons, by small changes and quiet rhythms. They saw him trimming the wild roses in spring, standing at the edge of the sidewalk in summer, arm raised in greeting as children biked past, raking leaves in autumn’s chill, and, in the winter, sitting at the window with a lamp burning, casting his shadow like a watchman’s silhouette over the snow. Some thought him lonely, but he did not seem so; rather, he seemed to be living in a time with different measures, where a day could hold the memory of a whole other life, and where the silent companionship of a map or a fading photograph was enough.

Once, when I was a boy, I lost a marble in his yard, a swirl of green and gold that I cherished more than seemed reasonable. I stood uncertain at the foot of his steps, the late light slanting across the porch, and Old Statler appeared as if conjured by my longing. Without a word, he led me to the overgrown hydrangeas, bent with surprising grace, and plucked the marble from the tangle. He held it in his palm, rolling it back and forth, and his eyes, catching the evening sun, shone as bright as any jewel. “Life is a great game of finding and losing,” he said, and pressed it into my hand, the warmth lingering long after I’d run home.

Mary had always been the quiet one in her family, occupying corners at gatherings, her hands folded neatly in her lap, eyes tracing the outlines of the furniture rather than meeting the gazes of those around her. It was not that she lacked opinions, nor that her mind was empty of dreams or judgments; it was simply that the flow of conversation rushed over her, as if she were a stone in the river, slightly out of the path of the current, only wet where the splashes reached. Her sisters, particularly Elizabeth, filled the rooms with laughter and the sound of swift judgments, and Mary could not help but feel that whatever she might say would be dismissed or misunderstood, so she said little.

This evening was like so many others. Their neighbors, the Bennetts, had come for supper, and two gentlemen were among their party. Mr. Darcy, tall and reserved, seemed to embody some unspoken expectation of the room, every movement crisp and deliberate. The other, Mr. Collins, was less graceful, performing a display of self-importance that would have been comical if not so persistent. As the conversation fluttered from the merits of various novels to the latest local scandal, Mary watched. She looked at Elizabeth, who sparred easily with Mr. Darcy, her words quick and light, never betraying the uncertainty that sometimes crept into Mary’s own attempts at wit.

It was not until supper had ended and the group dispersed into the drawing room that Mary found herself unexpectedly alone with Mr. Darcy. Elizabeth was engaged in a spirited debate with Mr. Collins in the next room, and the rest of the party had vanished into pockets of conversation elsewhere. Mary sat near the window, her hands resting on her book, though she had not read a single word since supper began. She tried to appear occupied, but she was acutely aware of Mr. Darcy’s presence, his silhouette dark against the lamp-lit wall as he surveyed the paintings with a kind of measured patience.

“You are fond of reading, Miss Mary,” Mr. Darcy said, his voice low but clear, carrying in the silence between them.

She looked up, startled, and then, feeling as though she ought to confirm something so obvious, nodded. “Yes, I find company in books that is not always present in conversation.”

He turned, his face softening slightly, the lines at his brow easing. “Much can be learned in solitude,” he replied, and she wondered if he spoke from experience or out of politeness. There was a pause, not awkward, but filled with the sense that something might be said if one only dared. “Your sisters are much admired in company, but you seem to observe what others might miss.”

Mary felt a blush rise to her cheeks, uncertain if it was praise or merely observation. “Elizabeth is much cleverer than I am,” she said quickly. “She sees so much—she says things I would only think.”

“Perhaps,” Mr. Darcy answered, “but seeing is not always knowing. Sometimes those who look more deeply understand more, even if they speak less.” He did not smile, but there was something kind in his manner, a gravity that made Mary feel as though she was not invisible after all.

They sat for a time in companionable silence, the room filled with the distant sounds of laughter and the clinking of glasses. Mary wondered what it would be like to speak easily, to have words flow without effort, to be noticed not for one’s silence but for one’s presence. She looked over at Mr. Darcy, whose gaze had returned to the paintings, and then at her own hands, pale against the dark cover of her book.

After a moment, Mr. Darcy spoke again, his tone thoughtful. “It is not always the loudest voices that are heard, Miss Mary. In my own experience, much can depend upon the quiet judgment of those who seem to stand apart.”

She found herself smiling, almost involuntarily. “You are kind, sir.”

He inclined his head, and she thought that perhaps he was not always as severe as he appeared. The sound of Elizabeth’s laughter drifted through the doorway, bright and unrestrained, and for once, Mary did not envy her sister, but felt instead a warm certainty in her own way of seeing.

The evening drew to a close with the usual bustle of farewells and promises to call again, but as Mary gathered her shawl and watched Mr. Darcy bow to her mother, she caught his eye and saw in his look a quiet recognition, as though they shared a secret withheld from the rest. She could not say what it was exactly—only that for the first time, she had been seen. And in that moment, it was enough.

Dear Clara,

I am writing this letter on the old wooden desk by the window, late in the evening. I think of you often and, as I write, I find myself wishing I could see your face in the flickering lamplight. So many things have happened since you left for the city two months ago, and I know it has been too long since my last letter. I suppose I am writing now because there is so much I want to tell you, and, though I do not have all the right words, I must try.

The days here are slower without your laughter in the house. The garden has changed almost overnight; the roses you planted have grown wild, sprawling across the fence as if trying to escape. Mother says the house feels emptier, though she wouldn’t admit it in so many words. I try to fill the silence with music, playing the old piano when the chores are done, but the notes seem to fall into a quiet that even music cannot reach.

I want you to know that I have read your last letter over and over. I keep it hidden in the drawer, away from sunlight and curious eyes. You wrote about the lessons you are taking, the city’s endless noise, and the crowded streets that never seem to sleep. You asked if I was lonely here, and I never answered truthfully. The truth is, I am a little lonely, but I have learned a kind of patience I did not know I possessed. It is as if I am waiting for something, though I do not know what.

You once said that knowing what you want is the most important lesson there is. I have thought about that a great deal. Some days I think I want to leave for the city and see the world as you do. Other days, I think I want only the quiet of home, the sound of the wind in the trees, and the comfort of ordinary things. I do not know which is truer. Perhaps both are, and I am meant to live between them for a while. I do know that, for now, I want to understand myself better, to listen for the small voice that tells me who I am. That is one lesson I wish you could teach me, though I suspect I must learn it alone.

Last Sunday, I went to church with Mother. The pews were half-empty, and the minister spoke about faith—how sometimes, when we cannot see the road ahead, we must trust that God is guiding us. I am not sure what I believe, but I do know the comfort of ritual: the way sunlight falls through stained glass, the warmth of hands joined in prayer, and the quiet moments after the last hymn, when everyone lingers before stepping back into the world. I wonder if you have found a church in the city or if you have left that behind, too, with so much else. I hope you have found something, or someone, to hold onto when the days grow long.

Father has grown quieter these past months. He asks about you, sometimes, but never says so directly. When the post arrives, he pretends not to notice whether a letter bears your handwriting. He spends more time in the fields, coming home late, hands stained with earth. I think he worries you will forget this place, but I know you better than that. You have always carried home with you, wherever you go.

I suppose I am writing not because I have answers, but because I have questions. I want to know if you are happy. I want to know if you sometimes wish you had stayed, or if your world is so wide you have forgotten how small ours can be. I want to know if the lessons you are learning are making you stronger, or if they are only making you tired. I want to know if you think of me, as I think of you, when the night is quiet and the city hushes for a moment.

Perhaps, in time, the answers will come. Until then, I will keep writing. I will tend the roses and play the piano. I will try to find joy in small things. And when you return—and I hope you do, even just for a while—I will be here, waiting by the window, ready to listen to all the stories you have brought back with you.

With love,

Anna

In the city of Athens, where the sun fell in golden sheets on pale stone, there lived a man named Timon. He was known to all, though few could truly claim to know him. His house stood apart from the others, at the edge of the olive groves, where the breeze from the hills carried the scent of thyme and dust. In his early days, Timon delighted in the company of friends. He opened his doors to all, feasted them, laughed with them, and called each man “brother.” There was no request he would deny, no jest he would not join.

But time is a wheel, and fortune rides upon it. When Timon’s wealth was spent, when his feasts grew rare and his laughter was tinged with worry, the city’s friends drifted away. He sent for one, then another, each with a reason for absence. Some wrote polite refusals; others gave none at all. A few, remembering past gifts, offered him only empty words and the dust of broken promises. Through it all, Timon waited at his gates, hoping each day for a change.

One afternoon, as the shadows lengthened, a stranger approached. He was a thin man, his tunic patched at the elbows, but he carried himself with a certain pride. “Art thou Timon of Athens?” he asked, voice steady.

Timon regarded him. “I am he. What dost thou seek at my door?”

The stranger bowed. “I seek not gold nor food, but a friend. I have heard stories of thy generosity. I have nothing to offer but my company.”

Timon’s lips curled in a wry smile. “Mayhap that is worth more than gold, in these days when old friends are cold and new friends are few. What is thy name?”

“Menander, son of Eudorus. I have come from the harbor. I saw thee once, in better days, when the city sang thy praises.”

Timon invited Menander inside. They sat beneath the vines, watching the evening come. Menander spoke of the sea, of trade and distant lands. Timon listened, one hand resting on the arm of his chair, the other tracing patterns in the dust. As twilight deepened, he found himself confiding in this new companion. He spoke of loss, of the bitterness that follows when one’s trust is betrayed. Menander listened, saying little. At last, Timon sighed.

“I have given much, and gained nothing. Is it the curse of Athens, that friends are fair in fortune and false in need?”

Menander shook his head. “Not all, Timon. Not all. There are those for whom friendship is more than a feast, who care not for thy purse but for thy company.”

Timon looked at him, searching for any hint of mockery. He found only sincerity.

The days passed. Menander returned, sometimes bringing bread or olives, sometimes nothing but stories. They walked the groves, speaking of philosophy and fate. Timon’s bitterness faded, though it did not vanish. He no longer awaited letters or knocks at the door. He no longer woke in the morning with hope, nor slept at night with disappointment. He let go of what was lost.

One night, as they sat by the fire, a letter arrived. The seal was familiar—an old friend, one who had once sworn eternal loyalty. Timon opened it with trembling hands. The words were polite, apologetic. The friend had heard of Timon’s troubles and wished to offer support—now, when there was little left to gain.

Timon laughed, a low sound that echoed in the small room. “See, Menander? When all is gone, the city remembers me. When the feasts are but memory, they write with fine words.”

Menander leaned forward. “Wilt thou accept his aid?”

Timon folded the letter. “Nay. I have learned, at last, to know my friends. Those who come not for gold, but for nothing, save a place by the fire.”

Menander smiled. “Then thou art richer now than in all thy days of plenty.”

Timon nodded, watching the flames dance. The night outside was very still. In the silence, two men sat together, and found that, sometimes, nothing is all a friend may bring—and all that thou may need.

The games were always announced with great ceremony, trumpets blaring from the city’s highest towers, banners unfurled along the avenues, and the people pressing into the squares as if to glimpse the gods themselves parading among mortals, yet beneath the spectacle and the laughter and the clatter of coins changing hands, Rian saw the same tightness in every jaw, the same wary flicker in their eyes, as though they all understood the truth but were afraid to name it aloud. For the games, though celebrated in public and sanctified by the Temple, were not merely a test of skill or luck, nor a harmless diversion to amuse the gods who, it was said, sometimes leaned from their seats in the sky to watch men contend for honor and survival; they were, in fact, a mechanism to sift the worthy from the wicked, and Rian, who had spent his childhood in the shadow of the arena, knew too well how thin the line could be between glory and condemnation.

It had always been this way, or so the elders insisted, telling stories as old as stone about the dawn of the city, when the gods, tired of chaos among mortals, decreed that every year on the eve of summer, the names of eight men and women would be drawn by lot from among the citizens and brought forth to play the games, their fates determined by a sequence of challenges so elaborate and capricious that not even the priests could claim to understand every rule or its purpose. Those who failed, who stumbled or balked or flinched at the wrong moment, were judged not simply as unlucky but as unworthy, their names struck from the city’s records and their families shunned for a generation. Those who won stood at the city’s heart in robes of crimson and gold, raised to heights they could never have imagined, their families honored, their children granted privileges beyond the reach of ordinary men.

But among the market stalls and in the quiet rooms behind shuttered windows, people whispered what could not be spoken in daylight: that sometimes the games were not fair, that the lots were drawn with a hidden hand, that the Temple’s favor could be bought or traded for a secret, that the gods themselves had grown indifferent or distracted by matters in the heavens and no longer watched as carefully as they once did. Rian had heard these whispers since childhood; his own father had vanished after his turn in the games, and though the official account named him a coward and a cheat, Rian’s mother had told him a different story, one that he kept locked behind his teeth, recited only in the silence of night when the city’s revels faded and the shadows pressed close.

Now, with his name drawn for the first time, Rian felt the weight of both legacies—the public one, full of expectation and pride, and the secret one, tangled with loss and suspicion—settle on his shoulders as he moved through the city toward the arena. The streets were lined with faces he knew, friends and rivals alike, all transformed by the knowledge that one of their own would stand before the gods and the judges. Some called out encouragements, a few made signs of protection, and still others averted their eyes as he passed, unwilling to gamble their own fortunes by associating too closely with one marked by fate.

Inside the arena, the sun was blinding, glinting off marble and gold, and the crowd’s roar echoed up into the pale blue sky. The other chosen men and women stood beside him, faces set in expressions of grim determination or barely contained fear. The High Priest, swathed in ceremonial white, recited the invocation, calling on the gods to observe and judge, and then the first of the games began: a test of memory and precision, in which each contestant was required to recall the sequence of ancient laws spoken by the priest and to inscribe them in the sand without error.

Rian’s hands trembled as he knelt, the memory of his father’s last words flickering at the edge of his thoughts, but he forced himself to focus, to push away the noise, the heat, the eyes of the city upon him. He remembered the stories his mother had whispered, the secret code she claimed was hidden in the words, something only the worthy could see, and as he traced the symbols into the sand, he felt for the first time a strange certainty, as if someone were guiding his hand. The judges watched, the crowd held its breath, and as Rian finished, he looked up, not at the priests or the people, but at the patch of empty sky where, if the old tales were true, the gods might still be watching, waiting to see which of the wicked would be revealed, and which could be counted among the worthy.

Marc Márquez has never been a rider to back down from a challenge, and as the MotoGP world prepares for another thrilling season, the eight-time world champion finds himself at a pivotal crossroad in his storied career. Having spent the majority of his professional racing life with Repsol Honda, the 31-year-old Spaniard’s recent switch to Gresini Racing Ducati has sent shockwaves through the paddock. For the first time since his emergence as a prodigy in the lower classes, Márquez stands as something of an outsider, his name no longer synonymous with the factory squad that delivered him six titles in the premier class.

The transition, however, has not dulled the intensity for Marc. If anything, it has reignited the fire that once made him the most feared competitor on two wheels. “This is a new adventure for me and for my family,” he said, his brother Álex by his side, now a teammate rather than just a fellow racer. “After everything we have been through in the last few years, especially the injuries and the difficult moments, I wanted to find a new motivation. Racing is my life, and to have my brother with me makes it even more special.”

The “difficult moments” Marc refers to are well-documented. Once the undisputed king of MotoGP’s modern era, the Catalan rider’s career took a sudden turn after his crash at Jerez in 2020, which resulted in a serious arm injury and a protracted recovery. Multiple surgeries, complications, and recurrent issues saw Márquez miss entire chunks of consecutive seasons. While Honda struggled to produce a competitive bike, Marc’s own ambitions were repeatedly thwarted by both his health and the machinery at his disposal. “There were times when I asked myself if I would ever be back to my best, if I would ever win again,” he admitted. “The mental side was harder than the physical.”

Despite these setbacks, the Márquez brothers have maintained an unwavering resolve. Álex Márquez, two years Marc’s junior, has carved his own path in the sport, winning the Moto2 World Championship in 2019 before stepping up to MotoGP. While Marc’s superstar status often put Álex in the shadows, the younger brother’s performances have steadily improved, culminating in his first podiums for Gresini last season. Their reunion as teammates is more than a family affair; it is a partnership built on mutual respect, healthy rivalry, and a shared desire to return to the podium’s top step.

Álex is quick to point out the unique opportunity this presents. “We know each other better than anyone. We push each other, we fight, but at the end of the day, we are brothers. On track, we are competitors, but off it, we help each other grow. I think having Marc here will make both of us stronger.” The dynamic between the two is evident not just in their interactions with the press but in their approach to testing. Both are methodical, pushing the limits of the Ducati GP23 while exchanging data and feedback, determined to extract every ounce of performance from their machines.

The switch to Ducati, MotoGP’s current powerhouse, represents a gamble for Marc. Gresini Racing, though steeped in history and passion, is an independent squad, lacking the full resources of the factory Ducati team. Yet the Italian manufacturer’s bikes have proven a dominant force in recent years, with Francesco Bagnaia and Enea Bastianini both securing wins and podiums. For Marc, the move is less about comfort and more about proving a point — to himself, his critics, and the broader racing world.

The MotoGP paddock is abuzz with speculation about what the Márquez brothers can achieve together. Marc’s raw speed is undiminished, as demonstrated during winter testing in Sepang, where he was consistently among the fastest riders on track. Álex, too, has adapted quickly, showing a fluid riding style that suits the Ducati’s aggressive character. Still, the competition is fierce. Defending world champion Bagnaia, Bastianini, and a resurgent Fabio Quartararo on the Yamaha present formidable obstacles. “This is probably the most competitive grid in years,” Marc acknowledged. “Every tenth of a second counts. There are at least seven or eight riders who can win races, maybe even fight for the championship. Consistency will be the key.”

With the season opener at the Lusail International Circuit fast approaching, anticipation is at fever pitch. The Gresini garage buzzes with a mix of nerves and excitement, mechanics and engineers working late into the night to fine-tune setups. The presence of both Márquez brothers has brought a new energy to the team, with fans and media crowding the paddock for a glimpse of the duo. A recent initiative to promote Hawaiian Sign Language (HSL) in educational settings has stirred conversation among the state’s educators, activists, and the Deaf community. Advocates say the effort to preserve and revitalize HSL is not only an act of linguistic preservation but also a step toward cultural justice for Deaf Hawaiians. However, challenges remain as the language, spoken by only a handful of native users, faces competition from American Sign Language (ASL), which has been the dominant sign language in Hawaii schools for decades.

The conversation reached new heights this spring, following the Department of Education’s announcement that three Oahu schools will pilot HSL curriculum in the coming academic year. The pilot program, developed in collaboration with University of Hawaii linguists and local Deaf leaders, aims to expose students to HSL’s unique grammar and vocabulary while promoting awareness of Hawaii’s Deaf history. The program will initially target classrooms with Deaf and hard-of-hearing students, but organizers hope it will expand to general education in the future.

Dr. Jennifer Lambrecht, a linguist specializing in signed languages at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, has been at the forefront of HSL research for over a decade. “HSL is a language that reflects the islands’ unique history—its syntax, its expressions, even some of its signs are found nowhere else,” she said in a recent interview. “While ASL is used by the vast majority of Deaf Hawaiians today, HSL is part of our cultural heritage, and it’s endangered. If we don’t take steps now, it could be lost forever.”

Lambrecht and her colleagues have spent years documenting the language, collecting narratives from the remaining native signers, many of whom are elderly. According to the latest estimates, fewer than 30 people use HSL as their primary language, and most are over the age of 70. At the same time, the state’s Deaf community—numbering several thousand—relies almost exclusively on ASL for communication, education, and public life.

The roots of HSL date back to the early nineteenth century, when Deaf individuals in Hawaii developed their own form of signed communication. With the arrival of ASL in the early twentieth century, HSL began to decline, as ASL quickly became the language of instruction in Deaf schools and the preferred medium in social and religious settings. For decades, HSL was viewed as an “incorrect” or “inferior” form of signing, and children were often discouraged from using it. Only in recent years has its value as a unique linguistic system been recognized.

Advocates for HSL argue that revitalizing the language is a matter of justice and representation. “For many years, Hawaiian culture was marginalized in our schools, and HSL was treated as less than,” says Nālani Kahele, an educator and member of the Hawaii Deaf Heritage Association. “Language is identity. Teaching HSL helps our youth see themselves and their heritage reflected in the curriculum. It says, ‘Your language matters.’”

Kahele, herself a child of Deaf parents, recalls learning HSL signs at home that were rarely used at school. “My parents and elders would sign in a way that felt more local, more Hawaiian. But I was taught to use ASL in the classroom. I think embracing HSL is also about reconnecting with our roots.”

However, the move to reintroduce HSL in schools has not been without controversy. Some parents worry that focusing on HSL could create confusion for Deaf students, who already face barriers to accessing educational materials and resources. “ASL is what my son uses at home and with his friends,” said Laura Liu, whose 10-year-old attends a Deaf program in Honolulu. “I want him to succeed, and I’m not sure what learning HSL will mean for his education or his ability to communicate outside Hawaii.”

Lambrecht acknowledges these concerns but says the pilot is structured to complement, not replace, ASL instruction. “Our aim is bilingualism, not substitution. We want students to be able to use both languages, just as many hearing students learn both English and Hawaiian. There’s a cognitive and cultural benefit to being able to move between languages.”

Funding for the pilot has been secured through a combination of state grants and private donations, with the hope that success will encourage broader adoption. The program will include professional development for teachers, classroom materials developed in collaboration with native HSL signers, and opportunities for students to participate in community events where HSL is used and celebrated.

On a blustery April afternoon, the wind turbines on Samsø Island spun steadily, generating enough electricity to power homes, businesses, and even some of the electric ferries that connect the Danish island to the mainland. The island, home to a little over 3,700 residents, has become a symbol of what’s possible in the global battle against climate change. Over the past two decades, Samsø has transformed itself from a typical rural enclave, reliant on imported fossil fuels, to a net exporter of renewable energy. As countries worldwide scramble to meet emissions targets and develop sustainable energy solutions, this small patch of land in the Kattegat Sea stands as a beacon of hope—and a laboratory for innovation.

“People still think it’s impossible to switch entirely to renewable energy, that maybe it’s too expensive, or too complicated for ordinary communities,” says Søren Hermansen, director of the Samsø Energy Academy and one of the architects behind the island’s green transition. “But we’re proof it isn’t just a dream. It’s real, and it works.”

The journey began in 1997, when Denmark’s Ministry of Environment and Energy launched a competition aiming to showcase the potential for community-driven renewable energy projects. Samsø won the bid, but the victory came with a daunting challenge: in a decade, the island had to switch from importing oil, coal, and natural gas to producing as much energy from renewable sources as it consumed.

Locals recall the skepticism that pervaded the community in the early days. “There wasn’t a lot of faith in the project at first,” says Karin Madsen, who manages a small inn on the island. “We’d been heating our homes with oil for generations. Wind turbines were mostly something you saw on the mainland.”

Key to overcoming reluctance was Hermansen’s approach. Rather than dictating changes, he and his colleagues at the Energy Academy held town meetings, answered questions, and listened to residents’ concerns. Ownership was a recurring theme. “If you want people to support a new energy system, you can’t just build it over their heads,” Hermansen explains. “You need to involve them. People here became part-owners of the turbines. They could see the benefit—not just in lower energy bills, but in dividends from selling power back to the grid.”

The first wind turbines went up in 1999. They were soon joined by solar panels, straw-fired district heating plants, and electric vehicles. Within a decade, Samsø had not only met its goal, but exceeded it: the island’s wind turbines generate more electricity than its residents use, allowing the surplus to flow to the Danish mainland.

Today, a stroll along the coastal paths reveals how deeply renewables have permeated daily life. Tall, white turbines dot the landscape, but there are also rooftop solar installations on schools, supermarkets, and private homes. Straw bales—byproducts of local agriculture—fuel district heating plants that keep houses warm through the long Danish winters. Instead of diesel, some of the ferries that serve the island are powered by locally produced biogas or electricity.

Beyond the technological transformation, Samsø’s success is rooted in a collective sense of purpose. “We don’t have big energy companies here, so we had to do things ourselves,” says farmer Jens Pedersen, who invested in a share of a community wind turbine in 2001. “It’s about taking care of our island, our land, and our future.”

The model has attracted international attention. Delegations from Japan, South Korea, the United States, and countries across Europe have traveled to Samsø to study its approach. The Energy Academy, a sleek glass-and-wood building overlooking the sea, hosts workshops, conferences, and training programs for community leaders hoping to replicate the island’s achievements.

But even as the rest of the world hails Samsø as a climate pioneer, local leaders warn against complacency. “It’s not enough to pat ourselves on the back,” Hermansen says. “Climate change is accelerating. We have to keep moving forward, adapting, and making our systems more efficient. It’s a journey, not a destination.”

The next chapter of that journey involves moving from simply producing renewable energy to creating a carbon-negative economy. “Right now, we’re net zero, in the sense that we export more green energy than we consume. But what if we could actually remove more CO2 from the atmosphere than we emit?” asks Jørgen Leth, an engineer at the Energy Academy.

The island’s climate roadmap outlines several strategies to reach this goal. Farmers are experimenting with biochar, a carbon-rich material produced by heating organic matter in a low-oxygen environment. When added to soil, biochar can both improve fertility and lock away carbon for centuries. Local companies are exploring ways to use excess heat from biogas production to dry seaweed, another potential source of bioenergy and a natural carbon sink.

As concerns about the accessibility of credit continue to surface across the United States, a new report from the Federal Consumer Financial Bureau (FCFB) is shedding light on the growing significance of credit scores in shaping the financial wellbeing of millions of Americans. According to the report, individuals with high credit scores are not only more likely to secure loans, but they also receive significantly better interest rates, especially on large financial products such as mortgages and auto loans. The report, released Monday, draws on data collected over the last five years and highlights the widening gap between consumers who have access to mainstream credit and those who do not.

The FCFB’s analysis finds that nearly one in five adults in the U.S. either do not have a credit score or possess a score that is considered subprime—defined as a FICO score below 620. These individuals often face not only higher borrowing costs, but in many cases are denied credit outright, creating barriers to homeownership, vehicle purchases, and even everyday emergencies that require short-term loans. “A strong credit score is one of the main gateways to economic mobility in the U.S. right now,” said Dr. Elaine Parker, a senior analyst at the FCFB. “Without it, people are effectively locked out of the best financial products, and that can have consequences that last for decades.”

The process of determining a credit score remains something of a mystery for many consumers, despite its considerable impact. While the basic formula is publicly available—it factors in payment history, credit utilization, length of credit history, the mix of accounts, and recent inquiries—experts say that many people do not fully understand how their everyday choices affect their scores. “Missing even one payment can cause a drop of up to 100 points in some cases,” noted Jason Lin, a mortgage broker based in Houston. “Yet people often think that as long as they pay eventually, their score won’t be hurt. That’s not how it works.”

For prospective homebuyers in particular, credit scores are more important than ever. The report points out that mortgage lenders are tightening requirements, and the difference between an excellent score and a merely average one can mean the difference between buying a home and being forced to continue renting. In the past year, for instance, the average mortgage applicant with a credit score above 740 received an interest rate close to 6.5 percent, while an applicant with a score below 640 faced rates exceeding 8 percent, if they were able to get a loan at all.

First-time homebuyer Ava Michaels, 29, learned the hard way how a moderate credit score can complicate the process. “I thought my score was good enough, but when I applied for a mortgage, they wanted to offer me a much higher rate,” Michaels recalled. “I ended up needing a co-signer and had to delay closing by two months to find one.” Her story is far from unique, according to housing advocates, who say that many first-time buyers do not realize the steep climb they are facing until they are deep into the application process.

Not all lenders weigh credit scores in exactly the same way, and some use alternative data in their underwriting. Still, the overwhelming majority of major lenders rely primarily on the traditional FICO or VantageScore models, which means that a consumer’s three-digit score can often be the single most important number in a loan application. Critics argue that this system creates structural disadvantages for certain groups, including young adults who have not had time to build a long credit history, immigrants, and those with past financial setbacks such as medical debt or short-term job losses.

Okay, so, honestly, I never really liked talking about my father. Not because he was some monster or whatever, but because, well, how do you talk about someone who feels like a ghost most of the time? I guess that's the thing about fathers—they're either too much right in your face, or they're barely there at all, just a shadow, you know? So you end up filling in all the blanks with stories you half-remember, or stuff your mother says when she’s tipsy and angry at the sink.

But, alright, this isn’t about her. This is about me and my brother, and, yeah, my father—Sir Robert. Well, not like "sir" like he got knighted or anything, more like everyone just called him Sir Robert because he’d walk around acting like he owned the place. And sometimes, in a way, he kind of did. He owned the land our house was on, a couple acres of rough, stubborn grass and some apple trees that never really bore much fruit. You could stand at the edge and see all the way to the river on a clear day, not that it was ever that clear.

My brother, Dan, was always saying how one day he’d be the one telling people what to do, not Sir Robert. He’d lift his chin and try to look older, and I’d laugh and say, "Sure, when pigs fly," and he’d get all red. Thing is, Dan was the proper son, at least in our father’s eyes. The sort of kid that always came home with his hair combed and his shirt tucked in. I was—well, let's just say, my mother sometimes used the word "bastard" when she was mad, and not always in a joking way.

It’s weird, how a word can hang in the air like smoke. You don’t want to breathe it in, but you do, and you can’t get it out again after. Sir Robert never called me that, at least not to my face, but he didn’t have to. There’s a way a man looks at someone that says everything, and it’s worse than any word.

So one summer, I was maybe fifteen, Dan seventeen, and Sir Robert started talking about the land. He’d sit out back in that old, cracked chair, drinking his beer, watching the sunset, and he’d say, “One day, all this is yours, Dan. You've got to keep it right, keep it in the family.” I’d be standing right there, but it's like I was invisible, like I was the wind messing up the grass.

Does it make sense to want something just because someone says you can’t have it? I never cared about the land, not really, but suddenly it turned important. I started spending more time outside, walking the edge of the property, picking up rocks, throwing them at the fence. I mean, who was I, really? The spare? The secret? Like, what would happen to me when Sir Robert died? Would I just disappear, like he always seemed to hope I would?

One night, Dan found me sitting by the old barn. He plopped down next to me, didn’t say much at first, just picked at the dirt. After a long while, he goes, “He’s just scared. That’s why he acts like that.” I stared at him, confused, because I’d always thought Sir Robert was too tough for fear, you know? Dan shrugged, kicking a pebble. “He’s scared I’ll mess it up. Maybe he’s scared you’ll want it so bad, you’ll take it.”

And I laughed, but I could feel something shift between us. Brothers, but not really—never quite equal. He was born right; I was a stray, a maybe. Still, we sat there, shoulder to shoulder, and for a second, it didn’t matter who’d get the land or who was whose son.

Here’s what I think: families are weird as hell. Who gets to count, who doesn’t. Do we stay because of love, or just because it’s what we know? It’s messy and unfair and sometimes it makes you want to run far away and never look back.

But, you know, next morning I woke up early, grabbed two apples—sour as ever—and tossed one to Dan. He caught it, smiled, and for just a moment, we were both just kids again. Not sons of Sir Robert, not “proper” or “bastard,” just two brothers, with the whole stubborn, scraggly land stretching out behind us, and the sun coming up like maybe today things could be different.

So, the thing is, I guess, when you wake up and it’s one of those heavy, gray mornings where the world feels like it’s been put on mute and the sky can’t even be bothered to look blue anymore, you get this weird itch to find some kind of pleasure, or—well, you know, I don’t mean anything fancy, just something, anything to take the edge off. I remember one such morning, lying there on my back, listening to the old fridge groan like it was just as tired as me, thinking, “Is this all there is for today?” But then, I don’t know, I think I realized something, or at least I started hoping I did, which is probably just as good—maybe better, actually, ’cause hoping almost feels like pleasure, too, or at least like a promise you gave yourself that you’re not totally lost.

I mean, people talk a lot about glory, don’t they? Like it’s this shining, solid thing sitting up on a shelf, waiting for the right person to come along and claim it, but honestly, who’s actually seen it up close? I sure haven’t, and I’d bet most folks haven’t either, though they’d probably pretend otherwise if you asked. I think glory’s sort of like one of those things you keep chasing, but even if you catch up, it kind of slips through your hands the second you try to hold on tight—like water, like smoke, or maybe like nothing at all, which is kind of irritating and, well, sort of a relief too if I’m being honest.

Sometimes I wonder, though, if we’re not just making up needs and reasons for things, just so we can feel like we have some control over them. Like, does pleasure mean anything by itself, or is it—uh, is it only a thing because we decided it should be? I guess what I’m trying to say is that sometimes, chasing after pleasure just ends up making me more tired than I was before, like maybe the chase is the whole point, and the second you stop, you’re forced to sit with yourself and your boredom or sadness or whatever, and that’s, uh, that’s hard. Maybe we cling to things that make us feel one way or another just to avoid feeling nothing at all—I know I do, anyway.

And there’s this other thing—I don’t know if this’ll make sense—when you want to please someone, it’s not always about them, is it? I mean, you tell yourself it is, but honestly, it’s so you can look at yourself in the mirror and say, “Hey, you did good. You made someone smile,” and that’s supposed to patch the day together. But, I mean, what happens when pleasing others starts to feel empty, or like, you know, more work than it’s worth? And what if there are days where nothing seems to click, no matter how hard you try—what are you supposed to do then?

Like, let me try and explain—there was this one time, not long ago, where I tried and tried to cheer up my friend, but everything felt forced, all the jokes fell flat, and it got awkward fast. I felt like I was performing on a stage with no spotlight and nobody in the seats. I kept thinking, “Why can’t I make this right?” but the harder I tried, the worse it got, until finally we just gave up and sat in silence eating chips, which, honestly, felt better than anything else I’d managed all day. Is that weird? I don’t know. Maybe that’s how things go sometimes—the more you push for some kind of shining moment, the more you realize maybe it’s not about glory at all, or pleasure, or making things perfect, but just being there when nothing is happening.

And yeah, maybe that doesn’t sound like much, and maybe it won’t ever be written about in a book or sung in some song about heroes, but sometimes, just sitting with someone, wishing things could be better but not pretending they are, feels like the best thing you can do. Who made the rules for what counts as glory anyway? Maybe some days, it’s just keeping your head above water, or sharing a bag of chips in silence, and not needing anything more than that.

You know, life doesn’t really unfold like you expect—it kinda comes at you sideways, and I guess that’s something you figure out early if you’re paying attention, which I mostly wasn’t, what with growing up in a town that people just sorta forgot existed after the railroad pulled out. And, the thing is, I thought everybody’s father acted like Mapple did, always standing in the backyard with one hand gripping the fence like the wood was gonna float away if he blinked. I don’t even remember when people started calling him Mapple instead of his given name, but it just stuck, like a burr on old wool socks, and so we just rolled with it, ‘cause why make a fuss? 

Anyway, Mapple just had this way about him—he’d star at the sky most nights, which was weird, except he’d be muttering about the stars and how they’d never point you the same way twice and how, if you listened, you could feel which way was north just by breathing in real slow. I’d laugh at that, sometimes, but not to his face. And, honestly, the more I think about it, the more I wonder if that’s not what he meant about living, like, you just pick a direction, trust it for a while, and try not to get angry when it turns you someplace you didn’t expect. That said, when’s the last time you trusted your gut about anything bigger than lunch, huh? 

So, yeah, Mapple wasn’t much for giving advice directly. He was—you know—one of those guys who’d spend hours fixing the same loose shutter on the house, all the while humming a song you couldn’t quite catch, and you’d ask him what he was humming, and he’d shrug and say, “Just something old,” like that was a good enough answer. Maybe it was. Some days I’d sit next to him, pretending to help but mostly just looking out at the grass, trying to spot shapes in the clover, and he’d say, “You see that tree over there? That one with the two branches like it’s holding something?” and I’d nod, ‘cause it did look like that—like it was cradling something invisible—and he’d say, “That tree’s older than anything in this yard. My old man planted it, and I figure, if a thing’s been living that long, it probably knows more about sticking around than I do.” That kinda stuck with me, you know? How could it not? 

There was this old paper map we used to keep in the junk drawer in the kitchen, all creased and smudged from coffee stains and greasy fingerprints, never got thrown out even when Mom did her yearly “throw out what we don’t need” campaign. Mapple’d pull it out every couple of months, spread it across the kitchen table, and trace his finger across the faded lines—never with any urgency or reason, just to do it, like keeping up with old friends. “You think,” he’d say, with this odd look in his eye, “that life could be charted out on something like this? Or is it just random squiggles, somebody else’s idea of where things should go?” I’d laugh, but I never really knew how to answer. Do you? 

Oh, and—wait, let me back up a bit—when I was a kid, we used to have this neighbor, Mrs. Lambert, who’d say things like, “You can always tell what a man’s living for by watching the way he walks home at night.” I didn’t get it at the time, thought it was just one of those weird old people sayings, but now I kinda do. Mapple, he walked slow, never hurried. Not even when it rained and the water was rising in the street, he’d just shrug, say, “It’s only water. Won’t carry me off yet.” That calm, it got into your bones, whether you wanted it or not. 

Now I’m older—well, older than I was, anyway—and sometimes I catch myself staring at the sky, trying to figure out if there’s a pattern to the stars that’ll tell me something useful. But every so often, I’ll reach for that old map, even though the town’s changed, and roads’ve been built over or faded out, and I’ll trace my own finger along the crumpled edge, thinking, maybe Mapple was right. Maybe you just keep going, let the old trees and faded lines remind you you’re part of something longer than you can see, and that’s enough. Or, well, maybe it’s not, but—what else do we have?

It’s strange how you can walk into a room you’ve seen your whole life and, suddenly, it looks different in a way you can’t even explain. “So, Miss Mary, you’re waiting for someone?” Mr. Blackwood’s voice always had this booming note, like he’d been taught to project across ballrooms and lecture halls, not quiet parlors full of anxious girls. Mr. Blackwood settled into the armchair by the fireplace, sighing loudly, as if the walk from his study had been some grand ordeal. He looked at Mary, still stuck at the window, and then at Elizabeth, and you could see him deciding which one would be easier to interrogate. “I’m told Mr. Darcy—” and here he paused, like he expected some dramatic gasp “—will be arriving this afternoon.” Elizabeth blinked, then bent to fetch the teapot, using the clatter of china as cover. “I hadn’t heard,” she lied, which was a bit of a shock, since I’d been there when the letter came, but maybe she just didn’t want Mr. Blackwood to feel like he knew everything before she did.

The sky was just as grey as it had been all morning; the only movement was a lone magpie picking at the gravel. “I suppose he’ll call on father first,” she said without turning, and then she sort of froze, like she’d given something away.

Isn’t it funny how everyone pretends they’re not waiting, not hoping, not dreading, when really, the whole house had been holding its breath since breakfast? Even the maid was polishing silver that didn’t need polishing, watching the lane out of the corner of her eye.

So, the thing is, nobody ever really asked Linton what he wanted, and maybe that was fine, or at least that’s how he’d tell it whenever anyone looked at him a little too closely, like you know the kind of look where you can tell someone’s just waiting for you to spill your guts and you just want them to stop, because what would you even say? So, you know how it is out on the water, when you’re the first one to set foot on the sand after a long night tossing in the boat? The air’s heavy with salt, and even though it’s supposed to be spring, somehow the wind finds its way right under your coat. Anyway, there was this guy—old Pericles, they called him, but only when he wasn’t around. He would come down to the shore around dawn, every day, looking all thoughtful like he expected some secret to pop right out of the waves. Honestly, I never knew what he was hoping to find. Maybe a message in a bottle or, I don’t know, a sign from the gods or something.

And then there’s Simonides. That’s me, by the way, though pretty much everyone just calls me 'Simon.' I’d like to say I was the village’s best fisherman, but that’d be a stretch—maybe top three if I’m lucky, and only because old Rhys hasn’t caught anything worth talking about in years. Still, I’ve been out before sunrise since I was a kid, so I suppose I know the ropes. Some days, I’ll tell you, fish’ll jump right into your nets, and some other days you’d swear they’ve all packed up and left the sea.

So this morning, well, I was untangling my line, half-listening for the gulls, when Pericles comes pacing up. You ever seen a man so lost in his head he trips over his own feet? That was him that day. He stops, stares at the water, then sort of sighs and glances at me.

“Simonides,” he says, and he always uses my full name, “you ever think about what’s out there?” He points past the rocks, toward the open blue where the sun is just starting to break up the mist.

Well, what do you say to that? I shrugged, said, “Fish, I hope.” 

He laughs, but it’s a tired sort of laugh, you know? The kind people use when they’ve got bigger worries than fish. “No,” he says, “I mean, really—do you ever feel as though something’s calling you from out there?”

Now, I’d like to say I’m the kind of fellow who’s got answers for everything. But I guess I sort of shifted my feet and mumbled something about the only thing that ever called me was an empty stomach.

Pericles just keeps on staring. “I had a dream of Thaisa,” he says. His voice gets real quiet, and I almost pretend not to hear. “She was standing on the shore, just—just over there, by the old willow. She called to me. And it was her, I know it was.” 

The thing is, most folks don’t talk too much about Thaisa anymore. She was his wife, or maybe more like a legend by now—disappeared in a storm, years back. Some say she drowned, some say she ran off to another village, but you know how stories grow around here. All I know is, Pericles never quite got over it.

So, I didn’t want to poke at old wounds. But I had to say something, right? “You figure dreams mean something, sir?” I asked, trying to keep my voice steady.

He smiled, that sad way he does. “Sometimes. Sometimes I think it’s just the sea, whispering in my sleep. Other times, I think… maybe I’m meant to go after her.”

Now, tell me, what would you do if a man like Pericles turned to you and said he might be pulled out to sea by a voice only he could hear? There’s not much you can do, really. I tried to joke. “Well then, you’ll need a bigger net, sir.”

He actually chuckled, a real one this time, and patted my shoulder. But I could see it in his eyes—he’d already set sail in his head, whether his boat left shore or not.

So, we fished. Caught two mackerel, nothing special. The sun came up, burned off the grey. Pericles wandered off by noon, same as always, and I packed up my catch and started up the path. I always pass that old willow on my way home. Call me superstitious, but sometimes the hairs on my neck stand up there, like someone’s watching. Is it just the wind, or do old stories hang around longer than we think?

Anyway, that’s how it goes. The fish come in, the fish go out. The sea keeps her secrets, and men like Pericles keep listening. And me? I just mend my nets and wait for tomorrow, same as always.

So uh, this is a pretty weird story, but you wanted one, so here goes. There was this guy, his name was—well, I’m not gonna say his name straight out because, you know, names have power or whatever, but let’s call him “R.” So, R was, you know, kind of a mess in the way that people get when they’re young and think they know how it all works, but I don’t think he really did. He’d wander around at night, just talking to himself, or maybe not talking, more like muttering. 

The thing is, he had this huge thing for a girl. And, ugh, can you believe it? Her folks hated his, like, ancient, grudge-style hatred where nobody can even remember why they’re mad. So, anyway, this guy—R—he would hang out under her window and sometimes throw rocks but, you know, carefully, because he didn’t wanna break anything. He’d say stuff like, “If only my name wasn’t mine,” and then get all quiet like he’d said something important. What’s a name, really, you know? Sometimes you start wondering if you’re just all the labels people stick on you or if you can be more than that.

I mean, how much do names matter? Like, if I woke up tomorrow and everyone called me “Zebra,” would I start acting stripy and wild? Or would I just stay myself and get used to being shouted at in a new way? That’s the kind of dumb question “R” would actually ask. And if you called him out—like, “Hey, you’re being dramatic”—he’d just sigh and look at the moon like it owed him money.

But, sorry, back on track. One night, the girl—let’s call her “J”—shows up at her window and she’s got this serious look, like she’s been waiting her whole life to say something. R nearly falls over seeing her, and starts in with, “What’s in a name?” and all that. He thinks if he could just drop his name, everything would be fine. Like, presto, all the problems vanish. But would they? If he was still who he was inside, would anything really change, or would the world just find something else to gripe about?

J shakes her head—she’s got this way of listening, but not letting him get away with stuff. She says, “Would you toss away everything for me?” and R tries to make some big speech, but he can’t get the words out in the right order. Have you ever tried to say something important and just ended up babbling? Happens all the time to me. Words get stuck. It's like the more you care, the harder it gets.

So anyway, the two of them go back and forth, and, honestly, it’s about as awkward as you’d expect. Love can be, what, clumsy? It’s not all perfect lines and swooning. Sometimes it’s just two people tripping over how much they wish things were easier. Like, wouldn’t it be nice if the world just chilled out and let people love who they wanted to, no drama? Ha—good one, right?

But here’s the weird part. R tries to make a promise—he starts with, “By thy name, I swear,” or something, then he stops and laughs. He says, “Wait, what am I even swearing by? The thing I said I’d give up?” and they both just crack up. The moon looks on, and, well, I dunno if the moon cared, but it was there.

You ever notice moments like that sort of float? Like, maybe they don’t solve anything, but for a second, you feel lighter, like the world’s nonsense doesn’t stick quite so hard. The two of them—R and J—they decide, right there, that love isn’t about the name or the old stories or anybody else’s rules. It’s about… well, nobody really knows, do they? Maybe it’s just about trying. 

So, they stand under the window, not knowing what’s next, but kind of okay with it. R says, “I love thee, whatever they call me or you or anything.” J grins and just says, “Good,” and honestly, that’s enough for the night.

That’s it, really. No fancy ending. Just people hoping the world lets them be themselves for once. Do you suppose that ever happens?

So, here's the thing: there was this old king and—look, I know what you’re probably thinking, another king story, but just hear me out—he wasn’t just old, he was also, like, tired of everyone’s nonsense. You could see it in the way his eyes drifted off whenever someone tried to flatter him. And, uh, he had this chamberlain, old as him, maybe older, named Mr. Giles or maybe just Giles. I’m not sure anyone called him “mister” to his face, but he had that sort of groaning dignity anyway.

There was a lady called Anne who kinda floated around the edges of the hall, always in dresses that looked like they came from another time. People said she was related to someone important, I dunno, maybe the king’s cousin’s cousin or something. She had a habit of smiling at everyone like she knew some secret. I guess—well, I guess everyone thought she was nice, but maybe not good in the way chamberlain Giles was good. You know how some people just do stuff for the sake of doing good? Yeah, that was Giles, not Anne.

The palace wasn’t fancy, not how you’d imagine. The floors creaked and the tapestries had moth holes. There were mice sometimes. Okay, a lot. The king tried to pretend he didn’t notice, but Anne always looked at the skittering creatures as if she knew they might just be smarter than most of the court.

So one morning, the king woke up cranky—like, crack-of-dawn, can’t-sleep sort of cranky. He shuffled down the main stairs (carefully, because, y’know, he’s old) and said—well, sort of barked—“Where’s my chamberlain?” Giles, who’d been up before the sun, shuffled in and bowed so low it looked like his back might snap. And the king waved at him, kinda dismissive.

I mean, have you ever seen two people who trust each other so much they talk in half sentences? That was them. The king would say “The thing with the accounts—” and Giles would nod and already be heading for the treasury. No wasted words. Anne would watch from the doorway, not getting in the way, just listening. Maybe learning, I dunno.

Here’s where everything started to go weird. The thing is, Anne—see, she wasn’t content to just stand there smiling forever. One day, when the king was distracted by arguing with his cook about whether salt belonged in porridge, she drifted over to Giles and said, “Do you think the king is happy?” What do you even say to that? Giles just raised an eyebrow and said, “It’s not my place to know.”

Anne sorta laughed, soft and kind of sad. She said, “If you were king, what would you do different?” Giles shuffled his feet, looked at his shoes. I guess he’d never thought about that because he just mumbled something about “doing good is more important than being king.” Was that wise or just obvious? Who knows.

Later that night—well, it was more like evening, but it gets dark early in autumn—Anne found the king alone in the garden. He didn’t look surprised, just tired. She asked if he’d ever wanted to run away. He smiled for the first time anyone could remember, which was honestly almost unsettling. “Of course,” he said, “but who’d look after Giles?” That was the closest he got to admitting anything, I think.

So they sat there for a while. The garden wasn’t much, just some overgrown hedges and one very stubborn rosebush. Anne picked at the thorns, and the king watched her, like he was waiting for her to ask him for something. But she never did, not that night. They just listened to the wind, and maybe the mice scrabbling around in the ivy.

The next morning, everything was, I dunno, a little lighter. The king grumbled less. Giles brought out tea for two instead of just for one. Anne smiled the same way, but now it seemed more, real? Something had shifted, like, quietly. And nobody said anything about it. Maybe that’s how things change, little by little, two people at a time. Or maybe it takes more. Is that silly? Maybe. But honestly, what else is there—if not small, good things that nobody notices except two or three people, and probably some mice?

So yeah, the thing is, it was one of those nights where you just know something weird’s gonna happen, even if you can’t really say why. You ever get the feeling that a place is watching you? Like, not the people inside, but the place itself, the walls and the windows and the floor, almost like it’s got eyes and it’s just waiting for you to do something stupid? That was exactly how it felt, standing outside that battered door. The light from the sign spilled out over the sidewalk, making everything look even worse—a little bit yellow, a little bit sick, and somehow dirty. I guess that’s the best way I can put it. And, honestly, I thought about just turning around and leaving, but then Ishmael nodded at me and it was like, okay, I can’t leave him out here alone.

Once we were both inside, it was almost too quiet. You expect places like that to be noisy, but it was as if the air itself got sucked out the second the door closed. I could hear Ishmael’s breathing, which was weirdly loud, and then my own, which suddenly sounded jittery and too fast, like I was nervous for no good reason. The thing is, I don’t even get nervous usually, so what was going on? I mean, it could've been the night, or the sign, or whatever rumor I'd heard about the place a couple years back, but most likely it was just my imagination running wild again.

Ishmael went over to the counter and tapped it, probably trying to get someone’s attention, but nobody came. I noticed a faded sticker peeling off the edge—it had a cartoon bird on it, but half the image was gone, leaving just a wing and a beak that looked oddly aggressive, as if it might peck you if you touched it. I almost laughed, but Ishmael shot me a look so sharp I forgot what was even funny. He whispered, “Do you see anything?” like maybe there were clues I was missing, but all I saw was dust and scratched-up wood and the ghost of a shadow flickering under the weird light.

And, you know, I started thinking—what if nobody ever came and we were stuck here all night? Would it get colder? Would we find out why the sign was flickering, or why everybody says not to go in after midnight? Those questions were rattling around in my head like marbles in a can. Ishmael shuffled his feet and looked at the door, then looked at me, then back at the door, and I could tell he was weighing whether to say something important or just keep holding it in, like usual. He finally cleared his throat and said, “Maybe it’s closed,” but his voice broke a little, so it sounded more like he was asking rather than telling.

There was a sound from somewhere behind the counter, like maybe a bottle rolling or a foot scraping. I wondered if we should just walk out, but the sign outside was still flickering, spelling out something or nothing, and even though my common sense was screaming at me, I felt glued to the spot. Ishmael, too. We just stood there, watching the place, hoping it would blink first, almost as if it was a game we had to win. I don’t know how much time passed—could’ve been ten minutes, could’ve been an hour—but eventually Ishmael looked at me and grinned, like he’d figured something out. He said, “It’s a sign, man.” And that was all he said.

So yeah, we left. The sign was still flickering, the place was still watching, and honestly, I have no idea if it was ever open at all. I guess that’s the point sometimes, right? You go somewhere, you wait, you look, you think too much, and you walk away, only feeling like you missed something you probably never would've found anyway.
