The whole thing felt like a set-up, like there was something we weren't told, y'know? So I just tried to keep quiet, but my foot kicked Linton's under the table and—well, that didn't help anything. He glared, and I mumbled an apology, which Edgar repeated back even though he had nothing to do with it.

"So," Heathcliff said finally, his voice gravelly, "I suppose we're all waiting for someone to get to the point."

Linton gave this nervous giggle, and Edgar stammered, "Well, I—I thought, um, perhaps we could, you know, sort things out?"

"Sort what out?" Heathcliff's eyebrows went up like he hadn't heard anything more ridiculous all week, and, honestly, I couldn't blame him. I hadn't a clue either.

Edgar straightened, and his voice got stronger, kind of. "Linton, maybe you'd like to say, uh, what it is we should... wish for?"

Now, I know that sounds kind of weird, but trust me, Edgar's always worrying about people's intentions. Linton tugged at his sleeve, thinking, and finally blurted, "I just... I wanted to get everyone together. One time. Like, maybe... mending things?"

Would anyone have guessed that's what he was after? Not me. Heathcliff snorted, and Edgar frowned so hard I thought he'd crack his own forehead. Me, I figured, hey, sometimes you gotta try, even if it turns messy.

Heathcliff leaned in, elbows on the table, and said, "You wish for peace, then? Between us all?"

Linton swallowed, hard. "Yes. If we could—just for a day—not argue, not fight... That would mean everything to me."

The thing is, nobody answered right away. It was just the wind whistling outside and, you know, Linton with his hopeful eyes darting around. Edgar finally nodded, but it was more like he was agreeing to something unpleasant, not a party. Heathcliff looked at him, then at Linton, and just shrugged.

"I can stay quiet," he said, "if that's what you want. But don’t expect miracles."

Edgar exhaled and said, "Well, that's as good as we'll get."

And then, for a weird moment, we all sat there, sipping lukewarm tea and pretending not to notice how uncomfortable it was. I wish I could say something changed, like a switch flipping, but, nah, we just managed not to yell for a bit, and sometimes that's enough. Linton smiled, small and tentative, and Edgar softened a little, and Heathcliff—well, he didn't storm off.

So, what do you think? Is it really possible to get people together and make them see eye to eye? Maybe, maybe not. But, anyway, we all left the hall that afternoon, and I think, for once, nobody looked back with regret. Or, at least, that's what I hope.

So, look, the thing is, I don't know if you've ever wandered into the woods at night, but it's not great for clear thinking. I mean, maybe you think you can handle it, but then the moon does this weird thing with the shadows, and suddenly every tree is—well, it's not just a tree anymore. It's some kind of, I don't know, like, guardian or trickster or, sometimes, just an old friend. Or maybe that's just me. Anyway, it was one of those humid nights where you can't really tell if the sweat on your skin is yours or if the air's just clinging to you.

So that's how I ended up, chest thumping, squinting between branches, and trying to figure out where Demetrius went. He'd said he'd be back quick. He never is, honestly, but I still waited. The frogs were loud. I tried counting the croaks but I kept losing my place, like, what's the point, right? So I was sitting on this half-rotten log and kicking at a patch of moss, thinking about Hermia. If I was being fair, I guess I was mostly trying not to think about Hermia. But, well, you know how that goes.

Then there was this flicker, not really a light, more like a small movement that your brain tries to make sense of, except it can't. I said, "Who's there?" and meant it to sound confident, but it came out kind of squeaky. Silence. Then a giggle. Is there anything worse than hearing a giggle in the forest when you're alone? I don't think so. I jumped up, almost fell over, and turned in a full circle like I was gonna spot something important.

"Show yourself," I said, and wished I hadn't.

A rustle to my left, and there's Puck. Not like, capital Puck, legendary mischief guy—well, okay, actually, sort of that exactly. He was leaning against a birch, picking at his nails. He had that look like he knew how the next five minutes would go, and, honestly, maybe the next five years.

"You lost?" he said, all casual, like people just appear in forests at midnight all the time.

"I'm not lost," I said, because that's what people say, even when they're lying. "I'm waiting for someone." Which felt like another lie as soon as I said it, but you can't take those back.

He grinned. "You humans are funny. Always so sure you know who you want, right up until the moon changes or—" He made this little gesture, like flicking dust from his fingers. "Or something else does."

"Where's Demetrius?" I asked, trying to sound bored. I don't think I managed it.

Puck tipped his head, eyes shining. "He wants Hermia, you want Hermia, Hermia wants—" He shrugged. "Who knows?"

"That's not true," I said, but even to me it sounded wrong. I kicked the moss again. The feeling in my chest was, like, tight. "If thou knowest everything, then what am I supposed to do?"

He laughed, but it wasn't mean. "Why ask me? I'm just the one who stirs things up. Choices are for you. Unless you want help." He squinted. "Do you?"

Did I? I tried to picture it, Puck fixing my life with a snap of his fingers: Demetrius suddenly forgetting Hermia, Hermia turning and seeing me. Would that even feel right? Isn't half the wanting wrapped up in the not having?

I shook my head. "It's not that simple," I muttered.

"Ah, but nothing true ever is," he said, and then he was gone. Not with a bang or a dramatic flash, just—gone. Which is maybe worse.

I stood there, and I guess I waited. Maybe for Demetrius, maybe for Hermia, maybe for nothing at all. The night pressed in, thick and warm, and there were more laughs—soft, like leaves, maybe just the wind, maybe not. If you were there, you might've heard me ask, real quiet, "What do I look like to you?" but no one answered.

And that's how it goes, right? You think you know what you want, you chase after it, and in the dark, sometimes, you find yourself asking questions no one can answer. Or, I mean, maybe that's just me.

So, I guess I should just start at the point where everything kind of went sideways, though to be honest, with us it always went sideways at some point, didn't it? We were a pretty ragtag bunch of friends, stitched together more by, I dunno, time and some shared history than anything else—like, nobody would pick us out in a crowd and think, "Oh, there go the best of chums," not by a long shot. Still, when Paul came staggering into the old café all flushed and out of breath that one rainy Thursday, even old Jules—who barely looked up from his paper most days—couldn't help but raise his eyebrows and say, in that kind of grumpy french way of his, "Qu'est-ce qui se passe, mon ami?" which just means "What's up?" but it sounds fancier.

Paul, well, he's the sort of man you want to believe—tall, got that honest look about him, though if you'd asked me last year, I'd have said he's always a bit too quick to buy some wild story. Anyway, that day he drops his umbrella, nearly takes out my espresso, and blurts out something about losing his job and, well, not just any job but his grandfather's old print shop, which he tried to keep running for the last, what, five years or so? The thing is, we all knew it was a miracle it lasted that long. We all told him to cut his losses, move on, but that's not the sort of thing Paul could ever do. Loyalty's a kind of curse for the unfortunate, if you ask me.

And honestly, I didn't know what to say. I looked to Jules, then to Greta—who was at that ancient game of pretending not to listen while she eavesdropped on the whole thing. She'd always said the shop was doomed, but she liked Paul, maybe more than she let on, and she surprised us all by reaching over, patting his hand, and saying, "We'll figure something out, won't we?" And maybe that's the moment when—look, does every group of friends have that one crisis when you just decide to dig your heels in and help, even if you know, deep down, you're fighting a losing battle? Or is that just the movies?

But anyway, we became a sort of makeshift committee right there. Jules, who hadn't moved faster than a tortoise since the Mitterrand era, offered up an ancient rolodex with names of "kind people, maybe, who remember your grand-père," though his handwriting was so bad that Paul couldn't read half the names. Greta said she'd bake and organize "some kind of fancy french fête," though she didn't know the first thing about actual baking, and I volunteered to redesign the window display, which, in hindsight, was not exactly the lifeboat you'd want in a storm—I'm more the talking sort, not the doing sort.

Days turned into a kind of strange routine—Paul moping, Jules muttering, Greta covered in flour, me fussing with colored paper and string in the dusty front window. Neighbors started popping in with this awkward blend of pity and forced cheerfulness, and, well, I suppose that's humanity for you: sometimes people don't know how to help so they bring you a basil plant or a six-pack, and maybe that does help, sort of. Sometimes the old men who hung around the square, who remembered Paul's grandfather, would come in and tell stories in a mix of French and, well, a kind of local slang that's half poetry and half nonsense.

Did it work? I wish I could say we saved the shop, pulled off a miracle, but life doesn't always hand you those clean happy endings, you know? In the end, Paul packed up the last of the type cases while we just stood there, all of us suddenly aware of how quiet it was without the old presses clattering. Jules raised his cup—wine, not coffee—and said, "To the unfortunate, and the very kind." Greta cried, of course, but that's all right. We left together, a little closer than before, I think.

And I guess that's what you get, in the end. Not what you hoped for, but each other—if you're lucky.

So, uh, the thing is, Alice didn't exactly expect her afternoon would end up like this. I mean, who really plans to be sitting on a jagged rock beside a weeping turtle and a feather-bristled gryphon that couldn't stop interrupting? Not her, that's for sure. And, to make it stranger, the sun's kind of hanging low, dripping through the clouds, painting everything that odd orange-pink that makes you feel a bit off balance, but in a way that's almost pleasant if you just let it be. 

"Soup's not all that bad, you know," the Gryphon said, tilting its head and scratching under its beak with a claw that looked pretty dangerous. You wouldn't want to be a mouse around that thing, Alice thought, but didn't say anything because, honestly, it seemed rude.

"But it could've been beautiful," the Mock Turtle sniffed, blinking tears from eyes so watery it seemed like they might just pour onto the beach and make everything even more soggy. "I always thought, if only I'd had parsley, or maybe a dash of patience, things would have been different."

Alice shuffled, her shoes all gritty from the pebbles. "Patience? Can you really add that to soup?”

The Gryphon barked—kind of a laugh, kind of a cough. "Shows what you know. Patience goes with everything, 'specially soup."

"And yet," said the Mock Turtle, and it sounded almost wise, the way old people do when they're telling you about how biscuits used to be thicker, "patience doesn't make it less salty, or give it any friends. I would've liked some friends."

Alice, not really sure what to say, poked a stick at the foam around her toes. "You have us," she tried.

"But are you friends or just, uh, flavor?" the Mock Turtle said, blinking.

She didn't know how to answer that. Who would? Are you a friend, or are you just passing through, picking up a bit of oddness before you go home and tell your cat about it? And the answer doesn't really seem to matter to the Gryphon, who's flapping its wings and sending a few stray feathers into the air, like it's shedding its worries one by one. If only people could do that.

"Well, what if," Alice started and stopped, because she wasn't entirely sure what she wanted to ask. "What if you could make any soup you liked, and it could be as beautiful as you want—would you still want someone to share it with?"

The Mock Turtle thought about this for a long moment, his shell reflecting the weird colors of the sunset. A seagull, fat and bold, landed nearby and eyed them all, probably hoping for crumbs.

"I think," said the Mock Turtle, "I'd want someone to taste it, so they'd tell me whether it was too sweet or too hot, or if maybe I'd done too much celery again."

"Yeah, and then you could argue about it," the Gryphon chipped in, sounding delighted by the idea. "Nothin' better than a good argument over soup. It's tradition where I'm from."

Alice kind of laughed, because she could picture her sister arguing with her about what should go in the sandwich, or if the jam was too lumpy. There's always someone who wants things just so.

"But," Alice said, more quietly, "what if they didn't like it? Or what if nobody wanted to try it at all?"

The Gryphon, for once, didn't have an answer. Instead, it just looked at Alice, its eyes a sort of muddy gold, like it was trying to see what she was really asking.

"It's a risk," the Mock Turtle said, and you could tell he'd been thinking about this his whole life—even if turtle lives weren't what she was used to. "But I'd rather try. It's lonelier to know nobody tasted at all, even if they didn't like it."

For a long time, none of them spoke, just listened to the soft flap of the Gryphon's wings and the distant slap of waves on the shore. The sun kept dipping, and the air felt cooler, and Alice wondered if she'd ever think about soup the same way again. Maybe she'd go home and make some—she wasn't sure what kind, or how it would turn out—but she thought, if she did, she might ask someone to taste it with her, and not worry too much if they made a face or suggested more salt. 

Isn't it strange, how you can sit between a crying turtle and a feathered lion-bird, and end up feeling like maybe, just maybe, you know a little more about what friendship means?

You know, I’ve always thought people talk too much about things they know nothing about—like, really, if you look at last night at Netherfield, who saw anything? No one. Everyone just guesses, and, well, they act like it’s knowledge. But, the thing is, I was there, just sitting by the fireplace pretending to ignore everyone else, when Lizzy came in—you know, with her muddied skirt and all that—and, I swear, there was a hush, just for a second. Not dramatic, just—like everyone noticed something but didn’t want to admit it out loud.

Mrs. Bennet, of course, can’t keep quiet when she feels she has an audience. “My dear Jane,” she cried—really too loud for a drawing room—“if Mr. Bingley doesn’t see how devoted you are, then, truly, nothing in the world makes sense.” And Jane just kind of smiled, polite as ever, but I saw her look down at her hands. Maybe she was nervous, or maybe she just wanted everyone to stop talking for once.

Oh, and Bingley was… well, he’s always nice. I mean, almost confusingly nice, if that makes any sense. Is it possible for someone to be too agreeable? Sometimes I wonder if he has any opinions at all. Like, he just laughed at whatever anyone said, fiddled with his cuffs, and asked after the weather—again. Poor Jane tried to answer every question like it was the first time, though Lizzy shot her a look that said, “Don’t encourage him.” Not that Bingley minded. I think he’d be happy if every conversation was sort of about nothing, just floating along.

And then you’ve got Darcy—well, he stood in the corner. Really, he only talked a bit, mostly to Lizzy, and even then, it was like every word cost him a penny. You could kind of see Lizzy’s eyebrow going up as she listened, but she never lost her cool. She never does. Actually, I’m convinced she’d argue with a thunderstorm, if she thought it was being unreasonable.

Honestly, sometimes I think the people in that room must be living in a different world than I am. I mean, do they really believe what they’re saying? All that stuff about happiness and good fortune and—what was it Bingley said? “Cheerful company is the greatest delight.” As if that explains anything, or means anything at all. Maybe I’m just being grumpy. Maybe I should’ve had more lemonade.

But it gets better—or worse, depending on how you look at it. Mrs. Bennet started talking about the entail (again), and I thought, “If she says something about cousins, I’ll run into the rain.” And Jane just sat there, patient, like she was bracing herself for a storm, but Mary piped up about ‘moral worth’ (whatever that is), and the whole thing drifted away. Are people really listening to each other, or just waiting for their turn?

Oh, and did I mention how Kitty sneezed—like, three times in a row? No one said “bless you.” Everyone just stared, and then it went on as if nothing happened. I guess that’s how it always is. Stuff happens, and we all pretend it didn’t.

But, you know, after the tea and the little speeches and poor Jane trying not to look tired, Lizzy caught my eye and grinned, just for a split second. Like, a real grin—not one of those “I’m fine, everything’s fine” smiles, but more like, “Isn’t this whole thing ridiculous?” And suddenly, I didn’t mind being there so much. Sometimes having someone who gets the joke makes everything else bearable.

So yeah, maybe nothing really happened last night, and everybody’s just talking because it’s easier than saying, “I don’t know.” Or maybe that’s how things move forward—one awkward conversation at a time. Who knows? I’m just glad Lizzy was there.

The new colony is called IK-3. It is sometimes referred to as “Polar Wolf.” Former prisoners and human rights defenders said the facility is known for strict rules and harsh discipline. CNN obtained statements from people who had served their sentences there. They described limited access to outside information and very poor conditions. Navalny’s allies said they are afraid he will face increased pressure.

Navalny’s mother said in an interview with a Russian news outlet that she worries about her son’s health. She told reporters that he already had health problems before the transfer. Mikhail Khodorkovsky, a former Russian oligarch who also spent years in Russian detention, made a statement about Navalny. He said on social media that prisoners are often sent to very remote areas as punishment. Khodorkovsky said it is difficult for lawyers and family to visit such prisons, which he called a way for authorities to cut off prisoners from the outside world. He called for more international pressure on Russian officials regarding Navalny’s situation.

Navalny’s lawyers tried to visit him several times in December but were turned away. They said officials gave contradictory explanations for why they could not enter the colony. Sometimes they were told Navalny was “not available,” other times they were told the prison was on lockdown due to quarantine. The lawyers said they are considering a formal complaint.

The Russian penal service responded to questions from journalists. They said Navalny is being held in conditions similar to other prisoners. They stated that any claims about violations of his rights are not true. However, activists said the secrecy and lack of access point to possible problems. One activist told CNN that when a prisoner is isolated so completely, there is a risk for abuse.

Navalny is serving a long sentence for what he calls politically motivated charges. He was arrested in 2021 after returning to Russia from Germany. In Germany, he was recovering from poisoning, which he and many Western governments blamed on the Kremlin. The Russian government denied these accusations.

The United States, the European Union, and other countries have called for Navalny’s release. They said his continued detention is a sign of growing repression in Russia. Russian officials replied these statements are foreign interference. They said Navalny’s case is only about following the law.

Navalny’s supporters in Moscow organized small protests. Police quickly broke up the gatherings. Many of Navalny’s top aides have already left Russia, fearing arrest. The political climate for opposition is tense. Ordinary people said they are afraid to talk openly about Navalny.

Khodorkovsky and other former prisoners said the authorities use the penal system to silence political opponents. The transfer to remote colonies is an old method. Even so, Navalny’s team said they will continue their efforts to keep his case in public view.

Navalny’s lawyer said he hopes to visit the colony again soon. He told reporters that for now, only official information is available. The isolation of the colony makes independent confirmation impossible. International organizations called for immediate access to Navalny.

For now, concern about Navalny’s fate continues. His supporters said they would not stop speaking about his imprisonment. Russian officials have made no sign they plan to move him from the Arctic colony. The world watches for more news from the remote north.

On Sunday, the first match at the city’s tennis open ended with an unexpected result. Pablo Andújar from Spain won against Dominic Thiem of Austria. Many thought Thiem would go on to the next round. The match lasted more than two hours. Both players were focused. Andújar started strong and took the first set 6-4. Thiem tried to come back in the second set but could not win crucial games. Andújar kept steady and won the second set 7-5.

Fans were surprised. Thiem was a favorite for the open. He had won important titles in the past years. His return to the court was awaited by supporters. After a long injury, everyone was hoping to see his best level. But on this Sunday, his game was not enough. His backhand shots missed often. He also made mistakes near the net.

Andújar said it was a hard match. He respected Thiem and knew the game would be close. He stayed confident after losing a few games in the second set. He said he trusted his serve and tried to keep putting pressure on Thiem. Andújar also said the stadium noise gave him extra energy.

Thiem told journalists he was disappointed. He said his form was not perfect yet. He promised to practice more and come back stronger. He thanked the audience for support, even when he was behind. Thiem said he would learn from the loss and not give up.

On the same day, two more games happened. Local players received loud cheers, but only one went on to the next round. Organizers reported happy crowds, even with rain during the afternoon. They said ticket sales increased compared to last year.

The next matches will continue on Monday. Players from different countries will fight for a place in the finals. For Andújar, the win gives him hope to go further. For Thiem, the tournament is over, but many think he can return to his best soon. The open continues with more surprise results possible. The fans look forward to seeing who will become champion.

On Monday, many people gathered at the community hall in central Honolulu. There was excitement and also worry. The Hawaii State Language Committee met to talk about HSL. Hawaii Sign Language, or HSL, has a long but quiet history. Few people know about this language. Many think that American Sign Language is the only way for deaf people to communicate. But in Hawaii, this is not the full truth.

Kaleo Lambrecht, who is 52, spoke to the group. He used HSL with strong movements. His mother, Lani Lambrecht, explained with her voice. “My son always used HSL at home. He learned it from my father, who was born in 1920. We did not know about American Sign Language. Only HSL,” she said.

Many deaf people in Hawaii share this story. Their families learned HSL many years ago, before ASL was brought to the schools. HSL is different from ASL. Some words look the same, but much is not the same. People say it is its own language.

Scholars from the University of Hawaii started to study HSL in 2011. Dr. James Green, a linguist, shared findings at the meeting. He said, “We have found that HSL is unique. It has its own grammar and signs. It is not the same as ASL. HSL came from the deaf community in Hawaii. It is a local creation. But now, fewer than 30 people use it fluently.”

Many who use HSL are old. Young people do not learn it. At the Hawaii School for the Deaf and Blind in Honolulu, teachers use American Sign Language. This is the national norm. Students there may hear about HSL, but they learn standard ASL.

Eileen Kamaka, who grew up deaf on Kauai, remembers her first time at this school. “I was 8 years old when I came to Honolulu. My home signs were HSL. But at school, all the teachers signed ASL. Other children already knew ASL. I felt lost."

Others had the same feeling. Some teachers told students that HSL was wrong. They said it was an old way and not correct. “This made many children ashamed of HSL,” says Lani Lambrecht. “They stopped using it. They did not teach it to their children.”

Now, people are trying to save HSL. The committee asks the state to help. They want classes in HSL, books, and videos. Some ask for HSL to be taught alongside ASL at the deaf school. There is hope that young deaf children could learn both.

The state has promised to look at the issue. Thomas Okana, who works for the Department of Education, said, “We know about the problem. We want to respect Hawaii’s history. But we must think how to add HSL. We have few teachers for HSL. Also, we must talk with families. Many parents only know ASL.”

Parents are worried about confusion. Some ask if students will become mixed up with two sign languages. Dr. Green says this will not be a big problem. “Children in many countries learn more than one language,” he says. “They are smart. They understand when to use which language. HSL is important for Hawaiian culture.”

The committee also wants recognition of HSL as an official state language. Some say this will help the language to survive. It would make Hawaii the first state in the US with two official sign languages.

But not all agree. Some school leaders say resources are too few. They say schools already struggle. “We need more teachers. We need updated materials. Adding a second sign language is not easy,” says Rachel Lee, principal of the deaf school.

Parents of young deaf children want strong support for ASL. They say it helps children to join in the wider world. “My son can use ASL to speak with deaf people everywhere in America,” says Ana Souza, whose child is six. “HSL is interesting, but he needs ASL to have more choices.”

But for the Lambrecht family, this is about more than school. “HSL is like Hawaiian language. It is ours,” says Lani. Her son, Kaleo, adds with his hands, “My grandfather’s hands told stories. If nobody learns HSL, those stories become lost.”

World scientists have discovered a new change in the reefs of the ocean. The research was released on Thursday in the city of Canberra. The study took place in different seas and focused on reefs. They found something special about sharks near these places. Experts believe the number of shark species is dropping in many parts of the world. Some species are disappearing from the well-known coral reefs. This is because water temperatures are warming. Scientists think climate change is the main reason for this.

The team has been observing the reefs for several years. During this time, many coral structures started to lose color. This is called bleaching. It happens when the water gets too hot for a long time. Without healthy coral, small fish and other creatures cannot stay. Sharks also leave. In some reefs, researchers noticed only one or two types of sharks remained. In the past, those areas had many more species.

This finding is worrying for marine experts. They say if this situation continues, the balance in the ocean could change. Sharks are important for healthy reefs. When there are fewer sharks, other fish numbers grow too fast. This can hurt the reef even more. Some experts call sharks the ‘guardians’ of the reef. If they go away, the coral is in more danger.

Besides temperature, scientists found other problems. Fishing is also affecting shark numbers. Even when fishing is not allowed near reefs, illegal boats come at night. They catch sharks for their fins or meat. Sometimes, sharks get trapped by accident in nets meant for other fish. The team says stronger rules may be needed. They also want people to learn about why sharks are important for the ocean.

The report also describes how weather is becoming less predictable. Storms are more powerful. When strong waves hit a reef, it can break the coral. After the damage, it is hard for new coral to grow. Small animals have trouble surviving. Sharks must travel farther to find food. Young sharks are especially at risk. They need safe places with lots of fish.

The research group used underwater cameras and special sensors. They spent many months gathering information. The team leader, Dr. Sarah Lin, said they saw big changes from year to year. She explained that in 2010, they could see up to ten shark species in one part of the reef. In 2023, only three or four were there. This makes it harder for the reef to recover after disasters like bleaching or storms.

Some local people are also worried. In the Pacific, islanders have seen fewer sharks near their homes. They say the ocean feels empty. Fishers catch less now. Tourism is suffering too. Visitors come to see healthy coral and big fish like sharks. If these disappear, there are fewer jobs for local families.

The authors of the study say solving these problems is not easy. The oceans are connected. Changes in one place can affect others far away. They advise working together, across countries, to protect reefs and sharks. They ask for governments to make new agreements and spend money on ocean science. They also suggest teaching children about the ocean. Dr. Lin is hopeful people will listen. If action comes soon, she believes reefs and sharks can recover.

Experts agree this is a warning for the world. Coral reefs help protect coasts from storms. They give homes to thousands of creatures. They are important for food and jobs. The loss of sharks shows reefs are in trouble. Scientists say everyone must care for the ocean, before it is too late.

A recently published report has caused much discussion in the country. The report, which was revealed on Thursday by the Commission for Inquiry, contains many pages about the homes for children and mothers that were run by various organizations during the last century. According to the report, more than 10,000 children and mothers passed through these homes. Many of them did not leave with good memories. Some did not survive at all. The commission said survivors told of harsh conditions, hunger, and sadness. Many suffered as babies.

The report stated that, in some homes, the mothers were separated from their babies very soon after birth. In some cases, no contact was allowed, so mothers could not see or hold their newborns. Some mothers reported being told nothing about where their children had gone. Some later discovered their child had died. Survivors spoke about feelings of loss that lasted for decades. The commission pointed to many failings by those who ran the homes and those who were supposed to check on them.

Among the findings in the report, the commission said that very young children and babies were often underfed. Many former residents described being always hungry. Meals were small and lacked variety. Some survivors said food was sometimes spoiled, or little was given to babies. The report said that this did not seem to be due to lack of money. Sometimes the homes received enough public funds for better care. The commission said the staff at the homes were often unkind, and sometimes cruel. Punishment was common, both for mothers and children. Some women told the commission they were forced to do hard work while recovering from childbirth. Some children described being made to clean large areas, or carry heavy buckets, when they were only five or six years old.

A significant part of the report concentrates on how children, especially babies, were adopted or fostered out from the homes. In many cases, adoption happened without the mother’s agreement. The commission said that records were badly kept. It is not possible to know for sure how many children disappeared from the records. Some survivors said they came searching for their birth mothers or siblings years later and found nothing but silence. A small number of people told the commission they discovered by accident that they had spent their first years in one of the homes. Their adoptive parents had not been told the real story.

The commission gathered information by interviewing over four hundred former residents of the homes, both mothers and people who had lived there as children. The interviews lasted several months. Many survivors spoke for the first time about their experiences. During the hearings, some women broke down in tears because the memories were too painful. The commission thanked them for their courage. Some people expressed anger, saying they lost their childhood to the system. The report contains direct quotations from survivors. One woman said, “We were never allowed to hold our babies. I remember the sound of them crying.” Another said, “They punished me for asking about my child. They said I should forget her.”

The government replied to the report with an official statement. The statement said that the findings were disturbing. The government offered apologies for the suffering caused. It promised to set up a special fund to help survivors. The fund will be used to provide counseling, support, and help with searching for information. The government also said it will consider changing the law so that all records are made easier to access. Survivors welcomed the apology but said that practical help was needed, not just words.

One particular part of the report has received much attention. The commission found that, in some homes, babies who died were not given proper burials. Records of deaths were often not written down. In some cases, the graves of infants were left unmarked. The commission said that mothers were rarely told what happened to their babies if there was a death. Other children who lived in the homes remember being told not to ask questions. Some survivors said that, as adults, they spent years searching for the graves of siblings or their own children with no answers. The commission described this practice as deeply upsetting and against basic respect for families.

The report also describes the living conditions inside the homes. Many survivors said that the buildings were cold and damp. Heating was poor. Some people remember sharing beds with many others. Privacy was not allowed. Mothers were watched at all times, even when feeding their babies. Several survivors said that children were sometimes left alone in rooms for long hours as a punishment. The commission expressed concern that the government checked the homes only rarely. Inspections, when carried out, did not always ask staff about the women or children’s well-being.

In the city where the excitement for car racing always runs high, there was a new kind of event last weekend. People gathered not only for the speed, but for something else too. Formula One was in town, but now it was not just about the drivers and their machines. There was a different mood because of environmental focus. Usually you would hear engines and see fans waving flags. This time, there were also banners talking about the planet.

During the opening ceremony, pop singer Goulding sang for the crowd. Many know her for her music, but here she also spoke about climate. She said in her speech that everyone has a role. Her voice echoed in the stadium, and many looked thoughtful. Later, she posted online about the event and the need for racing to care about environment. Some fans agreed, saying that sport can lead to positive change. A few thought it was strange to mix racing and environmental messages. They said it is not what Formula One is known for.

The organizers shared that this year they have new cooling technology for the cars. They said this helps to lower the heat produced by racing and makes the engines last longer. A spokesperson explained that the old cooling systems were not friendly for the air. The new ones use materials which break down better and use less electricity. Engineers also said that the cars have changed a little to make them less noisy and less wasteful.

Racing teams did not all agree about these changes. One team leader said during an interview that it is cool to try something new. He mentioned they have also started using recycled materials for uniforms and helmets. Another driver said he likes the idea but is worried about the effect on the car’s speed. He told reporters that Formula One is about winning. He wondered if these rules will make races less exciting. His teammate did not mind, he said it is the future and we have to change with it.

Fans noticed that the usual smell of burning rubber was softer this time. Some young visitors said they liked the cleaner smell. They pointed out how the track looked brighter. Vendor stalls also offered different food, with less meat and more plant-based dishes. One family commented that the choices were healthier and even better for the earth. They said they have never seen Formula One with so many green ideas.

After the races, Goulding attended a talk with engineers and students. She listened as they explained how the new rules work. She nodded and shared stories about her own changes for the planet. The students asked questions about what else can be done in racing. One engineer showed a model for a future car that will use less fuel. The singer laughed and said she hoped to see it soon on the track.

There were also critics at the event. A group of old fans said loudly that racing is about tradition. They do not like changes in the sound and smell. One man said he has followed Formula One since childhood and wishes for the “old days.” Organizers listened but said that the world is different now. They want the sport to give excitement, but also care for the air and water. They explained that more changes will come next year, including new rules for tire use and travel.

On social media, people argued. Some posted that this new Formula One is good for young fans. They are happy to see sports have a voice in environmental talks. Others complained that too many changes will make everything boring. They said they come for speed and danger, not for lessons. Both sides agreed that seeing Goulding at the racetrack was unusual but cool.

In the end, the event finished with a big cheer. It was not only about fast cars, but about what racing could become. People went home talking about the races and also about what they can do for the earth. Organizers said they hope the mix of music, racing, and environment will grow next season. Many wonder if Formula One will keep this new direction. For now, they have started something different, and many are watching.

Hurricane Doriana, which has been moving through the Atlantic since the end of August, hit the northern Bahamas islands with strong force during the first week of September. The first warnings were sent out by meteorologists early on August 28, when the storm became stronger. By the start of September, it had grown into a dangerous Category 5 system. Citizens in the islands prepared for the winds and rain, but some were still surprised by the strength of both. On September 2, towns in Abaco and Grand Bahama faced winds up to 290 kilometers per hour. Houses lost roofs. In many places, the water reached the second stories.

People started sharing photos online. There were images of empty homes, with windows blown out. Many photos showed streets now under water. Boats that used to float in the sea now sat stuck between buildings. The captions that people wrote for these photos said the same thing: this hurricane changed everything. Some pictures from August showed the islands before the hurricane. Blue sky, palm trees, children laughing by the water. Photos taken after Doriana arrived showed a very different world. In one, a man stands in waist-high water, carrying his daughter. In another, a group waits on a rooftop for help, trying to wave to a passing helicopter.

Rescue workers came from other islands and countries to help. They brought food, water, and blankets. The wind still blew hard as they arrived. It was difficult to land boats or helicopters. Some workers had to wait for hours before it was safe. When the wind slowed, teams started to check every house. They called out, knocked on doors, and looked for people or animals left behind. Many families lost contact with their relatives during the storm. Mobile phone service was broken for two days. People used radios to ask for news.

The government in Nassau said at least sixty people were missing by September 5. The number was expected to rise. Photos from weather agencies showed the storm cloud stretching far across the water. Caption writers explained the science: warm water made Doriana bigger and more powerful. Local leaders said it was the worst hurricane since records began. They said the islands will take years to recover. Officials compared before-and-after images and explained how so many houses were now gone. The wind flattened wooden homes in minutes. Brick homes stood longer, but many lost windows and walls. School classrooms filled with debris. Hospital staff worked almost without rest. They had to treat many people for cuts and broken bones.

International aid groups started to fly supplies in. United Nations teams gave out bottled water, crackers, and tarpaulins. Doctors Without Borders set up tents and treated those with fever or wounds. Volunteers shared more photos for the world to see. One photo’s caption described the silence after the hurricane, broken only by helicopters. Animals wandered the ruined neighborhoods, hungry and afraid. Survivors slept outside, waiting for help or news. In the evenings, families gathered by candles and shared stories of what happened when the wind came.

Many people wondered why the hurricane stayed over the islands for almost 24 hours. Meteorologists said Doriana moved very slowly, which made the flooding worse. In some neighborhoods, water levels rose by two meters. People climbed roofs, or took shelter in attics. Later, some rescue stories became famous. One man swam through wind and rain to reach his neighbor, who could not walk. He brought them food wrapped in plastic. Another story told of a nurse in Freeport who used her own car to drive patients to the hospital, even as water reached the door. Social media helped families find each other. Photos of missing people were posted with names and last-known locations. Some were found safe. Others have not returned.

After Doriana passed, officials counted the losses. More than 15,000 homes had damage. Schools, clinics, and stores closed. The main roads were blocked by trees, cars, and pieces of roof. Some residents started to clean up as soon as the wind stopped. They used buckets to carry water out of homes, and swept mud from floors. They hung wet clothes and blankets outside, hoping the sun would return. Volunteers gave out bread and water. In some places, there was no electricity even after a week. Generators became important. People waited in line to charge phones or fill water bottles.

Some people left the islands. They traveled by boat to Nassau or to Florida. Others decided to stay and help rebuild. The government promised money for repairs, but many said it would not be fast. Aid workers warned about sickness from the dirty water. They gave out medicine and taught people how to boil water before drinking it. The government set up shelters in churches and schools. Families crowded together, sometimes three or four in a room. Children painted pictures to show the storm. Some of these were posted next to photos from the hurricane.

A story has gained attention in Newport. A man is trying very hard to locate a hard drive, which he believes contains a large amount of Bitcoins. The man estimates the value to be near several million dollars. He says the digital currency was stored on his drive. The drive was thrown away by mistake years ago. The man thought he could recover the files. Now, he faces many challenges.

The man worked with computers and technology in the past. At the time, Bitcoin was not widely known. He bought the coins when the price was low. He kept his digital wallet on a drive for safety. He did not expect this wallet would later be so valuable. The wallet is linked to more than eight thousand Bitcoins. The worth has risen over recent years. It has become a big topic for people who follow the cryptocurrency markets. CNN has covered this search in several reports.

The man lives in Newport. He said he realized he lost his hard drive after cleaning his house. He mixed the drive with other trash and took it to a landfill. After discovering the mistake, he started asking officials at the landfill for help. However, the landfill has strict rules. The area is large, and many trucks bring trash daily. The drive is somewhere under thousands of tons of waste. Some officials are not willing to allow a search, saying it may cause health risks.

Over the years, the man has asked for permission. He has submitted plans to recover the drive. He said he would pay for the costs. He said he would share some of the Bitcoin value with the town. He met with city leaders, but his plans were rejected. Many worries exist about safety, pollution, and the costs of searching. There is fear the search might damage local land and cause more problems. The city leaders said the risks do not justify the effort.

The man tried to get attention from more people. He used online forums. He contacted news organizations. CNN and other outlets reported his story. Many Bitcoin fans offered ideas, but few could help with the search. The man offered rewards to those who can find the drive. Some volunteers wanted to join. Still, the city administration has not changed its position.

The man explained that Bitcoin can only be accessed with the correct private key. This key is stored on his missing drive. Without the drive, the coins are locked. No one can spend them or move them. The man said he has searched other places but found nothing. He believes the drive is still at the landfill. He is confident that, if found, the Bitcoins would still be on the drive. Many experts agree it is possible if the drive is not damaged.

As the story continues, people discuss the case in Newport and elsewhere. Some say the process of searching for the drive is not realistic. Others say it is worth trying, because the value is so high. The man said he would keep asking for help. He is not giving up. He hopes rules will change one day, so he can try again.

The case has brought questions about digital currency and safety. Many users are reminded to protect their wallets and keys. The man admitted he did not think about the risk. He said he regrets not making backups. He said he has received messages from people who lost coins in similar ways. There is interest in finding solutions to prevent more losses.

Local authorities in Newport have said there is no change in policy. The landfill is still closed to such searches. Officials say they are not planning to allow digging for lost items. They also say they are not responsible for private losses.

The man is sharing his story to warn others. He says he keeps watching the price of Bitcoin. He describes the experience as difficult. Many people continue to follow updates. Some wonder if the drive will ever be found. For now, the question remains open.

The football club Colo-Colo has become a topic of much conversation in Chile after their performance this season. Colo-Colo is known as one of the biggest teams in the south of the country. Their fans are used to seeing the team play at the top of the league. This year has been difficult for them. For the first time in many years, the club faces the threat of relegation. Many people in Chile are talking about this situation.

The team started the season with hope. The players trained hard. The club believed that their experience would help. The first matches did not go as planned. Colo-Colo lost several games in a row. The supporters were surprised. There was worry growing among the fans. The coach tried to change the tactics. The players worked to improve. Still, the results did not improve much.

Many people blame the problems on the club’s management. Some say there were bad decisions made about player transfers. A few important players left last year. The replacements did not bring the same quality. Some fans think that the club spent too much money. Others believe that the spirit is missing. Loyal supporters say the famous Colo-Colo pride is not seen this year. There are talks on radio and television about these matters.

The coach speaks to the media often. He says that the players are working hard every week. He states that the team is focused. The captain says the same thing. They promise that they will not let the club fall. The pressure is strong. The other teams in the league see Colo-Colo as an easy opponent now. This is new for the club. The stadium is not full for home games. Some fans are staying away until performance improves.

In the south of Chile, football is more than just a game. Colo-Colo has been a source of pride. Their victories brought happiness. Families united to watch the matches together. They hope that the players will remember the past and fight harder.
